column1: Section 2, table 2b: Audience Use Cases

The problems each audience faces, when each problem shows up, what we want to change, and the scenarios a product would need to support. Built from 412 caregiver posts and threads (303 Reddit, 109 forum). Rank 1 = the problem seen in the most posts and threads for that audience. Scenarios are our own wording of what caregivers said they want: open problems, not features or decisions. Problem = What is hard for them today? When it happens = When does this problem show up? What we want to change = How should it be different? Scenarios to support = What would we need to help with?

column1: Audience 1: adult child caring for a parent
column3: Adult children carry the care, often alone, and can't get a break even when help exists.
column5:
• While carrying all the care alone, often for years
• When cost, paperwork or a refusing parent blocks a break
• When siblings won't step in so they can rest
• While juggling care with work, school or their own family
column6:
• We want them to get real breaks they can afford
• We want them to have family or paid help that steps in
• We want them to cope with guilt and grief, and know next steps
• We want them to set limits without guilt or judgment
column7:
• Help them find a break they can afford and qualify for
• Help them get the parent to accept outside help
• Help them get relatives to cover time off
• Help them handle guilt and set limits they can keep

column1: Audience 1: adult child caring for a parent
column3: A parent's anger, confusion and anxiety make visits, calls and big talks hard.
column5:
• When the parent rages, argues, accuses or turns violent
• When new confusion or strange behavior appears
• When raising hard topics: final wishes, care plans, car keys
• When anxiety brings nonstop calls and questions
column6:
• We want them to handle hard talks about final wishes
• We want them to know if a change is the illness, and what's next
• We want them to calm outbursts and calls, and stay calm themselves
• We want them to be treated with respect, not accused
column7:
• Help them prepare for a hard talk
• Help them tell the illness from a new medical problem
• Help them calm an outburst in the moment
• Help them cope with nonstop calls without losing their day

column1: Audience 1: adult child caring for a parent
column3: Care costs, benefits and legal papers pile up faster than families can handle them.
column5:
• When care costs outrun savings, income or insurance
• When applying for Medicaid, benefits or caregiver pay
• When the parent overspends, gets scammed or stops paying bills
• When power of attorney and legal papers need sorting
column6:
• We want them to have legal authority and papers sorted in time
• We want them to understand and get Medicaid and benefits
• We want them to control bills and stop scams and overspending
• We want them to find and afford the care the parent needs
column7:
• Help them get legal papers in place before a crisis
• Help them find and apply for benefits
• Help them spot scams and missed bills early
• Help them plan how to pay for care

column1: Audience 1: adult child caring for a parent
column3: Daily hands-on care, meals and medicines fall on the caregiver.
column5:
• During toileting, incontinence and bathing
• While running daily medicines, meals and errands
• After a hospital stay or new health problem changes care
• When the parent skips, refuses or forgets medicines
column6:
• We want them to see the parent take medicines and eat safely
• We want them to know which medicine or treatment is right
• We want them to have safe tools for moving, healing and pills
• We want them to have hands-on help with care and chores
column7:
• Help them know medicines were taken
• Help them learn hands-on care safely
• Help them adjust care after a hospital stay
• Help them share daily tasks with others

column1: Audience 1: adult child caring for a parent
column3: The parent says no to doctors, help, moving or giving up the car.
column5:
• When the parent refuses doctors, treatment or medicine
• When the parent won't change habits or do therapy
• When the parent resists moving somewhere safer
• When the parent turns down paid help or aids
column6:
• We want them to get the parent to accept doctors or help
• We want them to see the parent take care of their health
• We want them to get the parent to accept a safer move
• We want them to find next steps the parent will accept
column7:
• Help them raise help in a way the parent accepts
• Help them try small steps when the answer is no
• Help them know when to step in for safety
• Help them keep going after a refusal

column1: Audience 1: adult child caring for a parent
column3: Relatives stay away, refuse to help or fight over decisions, leaving one person alone.
column5:
• While relatives stay away and leave all care to one
• When the other parent avoids or blocks care
• When relatives distrust, accuse or override the caregiver
• When siblings refuse to help, even when asked
column6:
• We want them to have siblings share the care and costs
• We want them to have relatives agree and follow through
• We want them to be informed, heard and able to visit
• We want them to get the parent the care doctors advised
column7:
• Help them split care and costs among relatives
• Help them reach and keep family decisions
• Help them keep every relative informed
• Help them show what the care really takes

column1: Audience 1: adult child caring for a parent
column3: Families must choose, afford and arrange a new home, sometimes in a rush.
column5:
• When deciding where, when and whether to move the parent
• During and after the move into a new home
• When a hospital or rehab stay forces a fast move
• While searching for an affordable place that will take them
column6:
• We want them to decide on a move in time, with family input
• We want them to find an affordable place that will take the parent
• We want them to find a place with caring staff and good days
• We want them to ease the move for everyone
column7:
• Help them plan a move before a crisis
• Help them compare places and costs
• Help them check how a place really treats people
• Help them settle the parent into a new home

column1: Audience 1: adult child caring for a parent
column3: A parent living at home falls, wanders or gets hurt doing everyday things.
column5:
• When the parent falls at home, again and again
• While a frail parent risks falling with no one there
• When a declining parent is left alone or wanders
• When cooking, pills or chores become risky
column6:
• We want them to know which risks to accept and what to do
• We want them to have fall alerts and ways to call help
• We want them to move the parent somewhere safer
• We want them to have hands-on help that prevents falls
column7:
• Help them find and fix the biggest risks at home
• Help them know quickly when something goes wrong
• Help them decide when home is no longer safe

column1: Audience 1: adult child caring for a parent
column3: Families wait for answers, get dismissed and hear about problems late.
column5:
• While waiting months for tests, specialists or a diagnosis
• When doctors dismiss or can't explain symptoms
• After care causes harm, often without telling family
• When trying to reach staff or get a callback
column6:
• We want them to get clear answers, causes and next steps
• We want them to get faster tests, specialists and callbacks
• We want them to be told quickly when things go wrong
• We want them to have discharge plans the family can handle
column7:
• Help them get clear answers and next steps
• Help them reach the care team and be heard
• Help them prepare for discharge
• Help them track what doctors said

column1: Audience 1: adult child caring for a parent
column3: Children who live far away can't tell how the parent really is.
column5:
• While living far away, unsure how the parent really is
• While managing care from another state or country
• When a crisis hits and family is far away
column6:
• We want them to know what is happening now and what to expect
• We want them to be closer, or able to help from afar
• We want them to have someone with the parent when they can't be
column7:
• Help them know how the parent is doing day to day
• Help them help from far away
• Help them find someone nearby who can check in

column1: Audience 1: adult child caring for a parent
column3: Children can't get into a parent's bank, phone or online accounts to help.
column5:
• When they need the parent's bank to pay bills
• When scams or misuse hit the parent's phone or accounts
• When the parent's phone or social media need changing
column6:
• We want them to get access to pay bills and help remotely
• We want them to block scam calls and account misuse
• We want them to change the parent's phone and online settings
column7:
• Help them get their own access to pay bills
• Help them protect the parent's accounts from scams
• Help them manage the parent's phone settings

column1: Audience 2: spouse or partner caring for a husband, wife or partner
column3: Spouses carry the care, often alone, and lose health, sleep, closeness and breaks.
column5:
• While carrying all the care alone, with no time away
• When paperwork and rules, often the VA's, block a break
• When grief or a setback makes the load heavier
• When they feel lonely, unheard or without affection
column6:
• We want them to have people who understand to lean on
• We want them to get real breaks and a life outside caring
• We want them to get through the paperwork to qualify for help
• We want them to feel close to their partner again
column7:
• Help them find a support group or someone who understands
• Help them qualify for help, including VA programs
• Help them take a break knowing their partner is cared for
• Help them keep moments of closeness with their partner

column1: Audience 2: spouse or partner caring for a husband, wife or partner
column3: The partner's confusion and mood swings turn daily life and talks into fights.
column5:
• While confusion changes the partner's daily behavior
• When a hard talk turns into an argument
• When the partner turns angry or aggressive
• When the partner repeats the same questions
column6:
• We want them to understand the behavior and how to respond
• We want them to have hard talks without blame or yelling
• We want them to calm agitation and keep their partner busy
column7:
• Help them understand what a behavior means
• Help them find words that calm instead of upset
• Help them get through repeated questions with patience left

column1: Audience 2: spouse or partner caring for a husband, wife or partner
column3: Spouses do hands-on care and medicines every day, sometimes with a partner who resists.
column5:
• While helping with eating, dressing and moving every day
• When the partner refuses medicines or washing
• When medicines are missed, changed or cause harm
• When handling supplies, devices and health tracking
column6:
• We want them to know how to guide medicines, eating and hygiene
• We want them to have the right medicines, given safely
• We want them to have steady supplies and daily routines
• We want them to stop being the only one tracking everything
column7:
• Help them learn hands-on care tasks
• Help them keep medicines right when they change
• Help them keep supplies and routines steady
• Help them share the tracking with others

column1: Audience 2: spouse or partner caring for a husband, wife or partner
column3: Spouses struggle to find helpers they trust and to understand hospice when it comes.
column5:
• When hospice is raised or begins
• When paid helpers are unreliable or hard to check
• While trying to arrange a break or leave them with helpers
column6:
• We want them to have a trusted helper and know how visits went
• We want them to understand hospice and get the care promised
• We want them to get a break sooner
column7:
• Help them find and check a helper they trust
• Help them know what happened during a visit
• Help them understand what hospice will and will not do

column1: Audience 2: spouse or partner caring for a husband, wife or partner
column3: Spouses worry about income, insurance and the cost of treatment.
column5:
• When income, housing or food is uncertain
• When dealing with insurance and treatment costs
• When deciding how to protect and control money
• When looking for pay or tax credits for caregiving
column6:
• We want them to protect their money and avoid debt
• We want them to keep a home, food and healthcare
• We want them to keep needed coverage and cut unused costs
• We want them to get paid and claim credits for caregiving
column7:
• Help them see what money comes in and goes out
• Help them keep their coverage and doctors
• Help them find caregiver pay and credits they qualify for

column1: Audience 2: spouse or partner caring for a husband, wife or partner
column3: Family and friends criticize, doubt or drift away instead of helping.
column5:
• When family or others criticize instead of support
• When family and friends ignore them or drift away
• When the help offered does not match the need
column6:
• We want them to have relatives who support, not criticize
• We want them to get real hands-on help and someone to call
• We want them to be listened to without being judged
column7:
• Help them show family what the care really involves
• Help them ask for specific help
• Help them find people who listen without judging

column1: Audience 2: spouse or partner caring for a husband, wife or partner
column3: Spouses wait and push for a diagnosis while their partner gets worse.
column5:
• After long waits or pushing doctors for answers
• When sudden bad news or a fast decline comes
• When doctors overlook key symptoms or the home situation
column6:
• We want them to get clear, timely answers from doctors
• We want them to have doctors take the whole situation seriously
• We want them to be warned how fast things can get worse
column7:
• Help them get answers sooner
• Help them show doctors the full picture
• Help them know what to expect next

column1: Audience 2: spouse or partner caring for a husband, wife or partner
column3: The partner denies their needs and refuses helpers, medical care or changes.
column5:
• When the partner denies needs or resists reminders
• When the partner refuses a helper
• When the partner puts off medical care or big changes
column6:
• We want them to plan together without causing anger
• We want them to bring in outside help the partner accepts
• We want them to settle who handles care tasks and money
column7:
• Help them raise hard topics without a fight
• Help them bring in help the partner will accept
• Help them agree on who does what

column1: Audience 2: spouse or partner caring for a husband, wife or partner
column3: Choosing memory care, paying for it and the move weigh heavily on spouses.
column5:
• When weighing a move, care options and costs
• During the move into memory care
• While the partner lives in a care facility
column6:
• We want them to choose good care and ease the move
• We want them to accept the move without guilt and stay close
• We want them to afford a place without losing everything
column7:
• Help them compare places and costs
• Help them make the move easier
• Help them stay close after the move

column1: Audience 2: spouse or partner caring for a husband, wife or partner
column3: Spouses fear their partner will get lost or hurt when out or alone.
column5:
• When the partner walks, drives or goes out alone
• While home and not closely watched
column6:
• We want them to know where their partner is
• We want them to keep everyone safe
column7:
• Help them know their partner is safe when apart
• Help them keep the household safe
